cards.q: What is the immediate first-line medical therapy for a patient presenting with suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)?
cards.a:
Aspirin 325 mg chewed (non-enteric coated) to achieve rapid antiplatelet effect.
Note: Oxygen is only administered if oxygen saturation is < 90% or the patient is in respiratory distress.

cards.q: What are the absolute contraindications to Nitroglycerin therapy in patients presenting with acute chest pain?
cards.a:
1. Right Ventricular (RV) Infarction (leads to severe hypotension due to preload dependence).
2. Hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mmHg).
3. Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitor use within the last 24–48 hours (e.g., sildenafil, tadalafil).

cards.q: What is the target 'door-to-balloon' time for a patient presenting with STEMI at a PCI-capable hospital?
cards.a: ≤ 90 minutes from first medical contact to device activation.

cards.q: What is the target 'door-to-needle' time for fibrinolysis in a STEMI patient when primary PCI is unavailable or cannot be performed within 120 minutes?
cards.a: ≤ 30 minutes from arrival to initiation of fibrinolytic infusion (e.g., alteplase, tenecteplase). Fibrinolysis is indicated if symptom onset is < 12 hours.

cards.q: Which post-MI mechanical complication presents 1–14 days post-MI with sudden cardiogenic shock, PEA, and cardiac tamponade signs?
cards.a:
Free Wall Rupture.

Key Features: hemopericardium, tamponade (Beck's triad). Requires immediate pericardiocentesis and surgical repair.

cards.q: Which post-MI mechanical complication presents 2–7 days post-MI with sudden pulmonary edema and a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla?
cards.a:
Papillary Muscle Rupture (causing acute mitral regurgitation).

Key Feature: Severe pulmonary congestion, often involving rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle (supplied solely by the PDA).

cards.q: Which post-MI complication presents 3–5 days post-MI with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and an oxygen saturation step-up from the right atrium to the right ventricle?
cards.a:
Interventricular Septum Rupture (Ventricular Septal Defect).

Key Feature: Left-to-right shunt detectable via oxygen saturation measurements during right heart catheterization.

cards.q: What post-MI complication presents weeks to months later with persistent ST-segment elevation, progressive heart failure, and risk of mural thrombus formation?
cards.a:
Left Ventricular Aneurysm.

Key Feature: Outpocketing of thin, dyskinetic myocardium visible on echocardiography. Warfarin is indicated if mural thrombus is present.

cards.q: What is Dressler Syndrome, and what is the preferred first-line therapy?
cards.a:
An autoimmune-mediated post-MI pericarditis occurring 2–10 weeks after myocardial infarction.

First-line Treatment: High-dose Aspirin + Colchicine.
Note: Standard NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) are avoided post-MI as they interfere with myocardial scar healing.

cards.q: Contrast Systolic vs. Diastolic Heart Failure by Ejection Fraction (EF) and pathophysiological mechanism.
cards.a:
• Systolic HF (HFrEF): EF ≤ 40%. Decreased myocardial contractility/dilated ventricle (e.g., post-MI).
• Diastolic HF (HFpEF): EF ≥ 50%. Impaired ventricular compliance/stiff ventricle (e.g., chronic HTN, amyloidosis).

cards.q: List the classes of medications proven to reduce mortality in patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF).
cards.a:
1. ACE Inhibitors / ARBs
2. Beta-Blockers (specifically: Carvedilol, Metoprolol Succinate, or Bisoprolol)
3. Aldosterone Antagonists (Spironolactone, Eplerenone)
4. SGLT2 Inhibitors (Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin)
5. ARNI (Sacubitril/Valsartan)
6. Hydralazine + Isosorbide Dinitrate (specifically in African American patients with persistent NYHA Class III-IV symptoms).

cards.q: Which heart failure medications improve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations but do NOT improve overall survival/mortality?
cards.a:
• Loop Diuretics (e.g., Furosemide, Bumetanide)
• Digoxin

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Sacubitril/Valsartan (ARNI) therapy in HFrEF?
cards.a:
• Sacubitril: Inhibits neprilysin, preventing the breakdown of beneficial vasoactive peptides (ANP, BNP, bradykinin) → vasodilation, natriuresis.
• Valsartan: Blocks the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor → opposes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.

cards.q: What are the classic clinical signs and ECG findings associated with Digoxin toxicity?
cards.a:
• Clinical Signs: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, and yellow-green visual halos.
• ECG Findings: Downsloping ST depression ('scooped' ST segments), prolonged PR, shortened QT, and ventricular arrhythmias (bidirectional VT).
Note: Hypokalemia predisposes to digoxin toxicity because digoxin competes with potassium for binding to the \(Na^+/K^+\) ATPase.

cards.q: What is the management strategy for Atrial Fibrillation based on rate control vs. rhythm control?
cards.a:
• Rate Control (Beta-blockers, Diltiazem/Verapamil, Digoxin) is the standard first-line strategy. There is no survival advantage of rhythm control over rate control for most patients.
• Rhythm Control (Amiodarone, Flecainide, Dofetilide, cardioversion) is reserved for persistent symptoms, inability to achieve rate control, or active heart failure.

cards.q: Define the CHA\(_2\)DS\(_2\)-VASc score criteria and the threshold for initiating oral anticoagulation in Atrial Fibrillation.
cards.a:
• C: Congestive HF (1 pt)
• H: Hypertension (1 pt)
• A\(_2\): Age ≥ 75 (2 pts)
• D: Diabetes (1 pt)
• S\(_2\): Stroke/TIA/Thromboembolism history (2 pts)
• V: Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) (1 pt)
• A: Age 65–74 (1 pt)
• Sc: Sex category Female (1 pt)

Threshold: Oral anticoagulation (DOACs preferred) is recommended for score ≥ 2 in males or ≥ 3 in females.

cards.q: Why are Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) preferred over Warfarin in non-valvular Atrial Fibrillation?
cards.a: DOACs (Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran) carry a lower risk of intracranial hemorrhage, do not require routine coagulation monitoring (INR), and have fewer dietary/drug interactions.

cards.q: What are the classic ECG features of Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?
cards.a:
1. Shortened PR interval (< 120 ms).
2. Delta wave (slurred upstroke of the QRS complex).
3. Widened QRS duration (> 120 ms).
Pathophysiology: Conduction through an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypassing the AV node.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) presenting with rapid, irregular Atrial Fibrillation?
cards.a:
• Hemodynamically unstable: Immediate synchronized cardioversion.
• Hemodynamically stable: IV Procainamide or Ibutilide.
Contraindicated: AV nodal blocking agents (Beta-blockers, Calcium channel blockers, Digoxin, Adenosine) as they promote conduction down the accessory pathway, potentially causing ventricular fibrillation.

cards.q: What is the emergency treatment of choice for a patient presenting with Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) or Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)?
cards.a:
Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation (high-energy shock) followed by CPR.
Note: In contrast, hemodynamically unstable patients with a *pulse* (e.g., VT with pulse) receive *synchronized* cardioversion.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic evaluation and treatment of choice for Torsades de Pointes?
cards.a:
• ECG: Polymorphic VT with a continuous twisting of QRS complexes around the baseline.
• Treatment: IV Magnesium Sulfate (first-line, even if serum magnesium is normal) + withdrawal of QT-prolonging drugs.

cards.q: How do you distinguish Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) from Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block on ECG?
cards.a:
• Mobitz I: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval until a QRS complex is dropped (dropped beat). Typically benign; localized to the AV node.
• Mobitz II: Constant PR interval followed by a sudden, unexpected dropped QRS complex. High risk of progression to complete heart block; localized below the AV node (His-Purkinje system) and requires a pacemaker.

cards.q: What clinical and ECG findings define Third-degree (Complete) Heart Block?
cards.a:
• ECG: Complete dissociation between P waves (atrial rate ~100 bpm) and QRS complexes (junctional/ventricular escape rate 30–40 bpm). PR interval varies randomly.
• Clinical: Bradycardia, syncope, and cannon 'a' waves in the jugular venous pulse (due to RA contracting against a closed tricuspid valve). Requires a permanent pacemaker.

cards.q: Describe the classic murmur of Aortic Stenosis and its key physical exam findings.
cards.a:
• Murmur: Harsh, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the 2nd right intercostal space, radiating to the carotid arteries.
• Exam findings: Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid pulses), soft/absent S2, and late-peaking murmur (indicating severe stenosis).
• SAD symptoms: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea.

cards.q: Describe the classic murmur and radiation of Mitral Regurgitation.
cards.a:
• Murmur: Blowing, holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex.
• Radiation: Radiates to the left axilla.
Note: Murmur intensity increases with handgrip (increased afterload) and squatting (increased preload).

cards.q: What are the auscultatory findings in Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP), and how does preload alteration affect them?
cards.a:
• Findings: A mid-systolic click followed by a late-systolic murmur at the apex.
• Preload reduction (Valsalva, Standing): Click and murmur occur earlier in systole (smaller LV volume leads to earlier leaflet prolapse).
• Preload elevation (Squatting): Click and murmur occur later (larger LV delays prolapse).

cards.q: Describe the classic murmur and peripheral exam signs of Aortic Regurgitation.
cards.a:
• Murmur: High-pitched, blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard at the left sternal border (third intercostal space) with the patient leaning forward.
• Peripheral Signs: Wide pulse pressure, Water-hammer pulse (rapid upstroke and collapse), head bobbing with systole (de Musset sign), and capillary pulsations in nail beds (Quincke's pulse).

cards.q: Describe the auscultatory features and primary etiology of Mitral Stenosis.
cards.a:
• Murmur: Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble best heard at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position, preceded by a loud S1 and a high-pitched opening snap.
• Etiology: Almost exclusively caused by Rheumatic Heart Disease.
Note: A shorter A2-to-opening snap interval indicates more severe stenosis.

cards.q: How do you differentiate the murmur of Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) from Aortic Stenosis (AS)?
cards.a:
• Murmur: Both are systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmurs.
• HOCM murmur: Increases with Valsalva / Standing (decreased preload worsens outflow tract obstruction) and decreases with Squatting / Handgrip.
• AS murmur: Decreases with Valsalva / Standing (decreased flow across the stenotic valve) and increases with Squatting.

cards.q: What are the ECG stages and diagnostic features of Acute Pericarditis?
cards.a:
• ECG Features: Widespread, diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression (PR elevation in lead aVR).
• Clinical: Pleuritic chest pain that is relieved by sitting up and leaning forward; pericardial friction rub.

cards.q: What is the first-line therapy for acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis?
cards.a:
NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) or Aspirin + Colchicine.
Note: Colchicine is added to reduce the rate of recurrent pericarditis. Glucocorticoids are second-line and reserved for contraindications to NSAIDs or autoimmune causes.

cards.q: What diagnostic findings and clinical signs are associated with Cardiac Tamponade?
cards.a:
• Beck's Triad: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, elevated JVD.
• Echocardiography: Diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle, respiratory variation in transvalvular flow.
• ECG: Low voltage QRS and electrical alternans (due to heart swinging back and forth in fluid).

cards.q: Define Pulsus Paradoxus and explain its pathophysiology.
cards.a:
A drop in systolic blood pressure > 10 mmHg during inspiration.

Pathophysiology: During inspiration, increased venous return distends the right ventricle. In cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis, the rigid pericardium prevents outward expansion, forcing the interventricular septum to bulge into the left ventricle. This decreases LV filling, stroke volume, and systolic BP.

cards.q: What clinical features differentiate Constrictive Pericarditis from Restrictive Cardiomyopathy?
cards.a:
• Constrictive Pericarditis: Calcification of the pericardium on CXR/CT, pericardial knock (early diastolic sound), and Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical rise in JVP during inspiration).
• Restrictive Cardiomyopathy: Normal pericardial thickness, biopsy shows amyloid/sarcoid/iron deposition, BNP is typically much higher.

cards.q: What is the definition of Hypertension based on 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines?
cards.a:
• Stage 1: Systolic 130–139 mmHg OR Diastolic 80–89 mmHg.
• Stage 2: Systolic ≥ 140 mmHg OR Diastolic ≥ 90 mmHg.
Diagnosis: Requires ≥ 2 readings on ≥ 2 separate occasions.

cards.q: What are the first-line antihypertensive drug classes for the general non-black population?
cards.a:
1. Thiazide Diuretics (e.g., Chlorthalidone, Hydrochlorothiazide)
2. ACE Inhibitors / ARBs
3. Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Amlodipine)

cards.q: Name the metabolic side effects of Thiazide Diuretics.
cards.a:
• Elevated (Hyper-): Hyperglycemia, Hyperuricemia (can trigger gout), Hypercalcemia, Hyperlipidemia.
• Decreased (Hypo-): Hypokalemia, Hyponatremia, Hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Name the key side effects of Loop Diuretics (e.g., Furosemide).
cards.a: Hypokalemia, Hyponatremia, Hypocalcemia (unlike thiazides, loops lose calcium), Ototoxicity (especially when combined with aminoglycosides), and acute kidney injury.

cards.q: What are the characteristic side effects of dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Amlodipine)?
cards.a: Peripheral edema (due to preferential precapillary vasodilation), flushing, headache, and reflex tachycardia.

cards.q: Why are ACE Inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis?
cards.a: Bilateral renal artery stenosis reduces renal perfusion pressure, making GFR dependent on Angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction of the efferent arteriole. Dilation of the efferent arteriole by ACE inhibitors/ARBs drops filtration pressure, causing acute kidney injury (precipitous drop in GFR).

cards.q: Define the Modified Duke Criteria for Infective Endocarditis (IE).
cards.a:
• Major Criteria:
1. Positive blood cultures for typical organisms (e.g., S. aureus, S. viridans) from 2 separate cultures.
2. Echocardiogram showing vegetation, abscess, or new valvular regurgitation.
• Minor Criteria: Predisposing condition (IVDU, prosthetic valve), fever ≥ 38°C, vascular phenomena (emboli, Janeway lesions), immunologic phenomena (Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, RF), microbiological evidence (1 positive culture).

cards.q: Identify the physical exam findings of Infective Endocarditis: Janeway Lesions vs. Osler Nodes.
cards.a:
• Janeway Lesions: Flat, erythematous, painless macules on the palms/soles (due to septic microemboli).
• Osler Nodes: Raised, painful, tender erythematous nodules on the pads of fingers/toes (immune-complex mediated).

cards.q: Which patients require antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures to prevent Infective Endocarditis?
cards.a:
Prophylaxis (Amoxicillin 2g PO 1 hour before procedure) is indicated only for:
1. Prosthetic heart valves or prosthetic material used for valve repair.
2. History of Infective Endocarditis.
3. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease.
4. Cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic imaging strategy of choice for suspected Aortic Dissection?
cards.a:
• Hemodynamically stable: CT Angiography of the chest and abdomen (gold standard).
• Hemodynamically unstable or severe renal failure: Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE) (done at bedside).

cards.q: Describe the classification and management of Stanford Type A vs. Type B Aortic Dissections.
cards.a:
• Stanford Type A: Involves the ascending aorta. Treatment: Immediate surgical emergency.
• Stanford Type B: Confined to the descending aorta. Treatment: Medical management first-line with IV Beta-blockers (e.g., Esmolol, Labetalol) to reduce blood pressure (target systolic 100–120 mmHg) and heart rate (target < 60 bpm).

cards.q: What are the USPSTF screening guidelines for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)?
cards.a: One-time screening with abdominal ultrasound for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked (defined as ≥ 100 lifetime cigarettes).

cards.q: What are the indications for surgical repair of an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)?
cards.a:
1. Aneurysm diameter ≥ 5.5 cm.
2. Rapid expansion rate (> 0.5 cm in 6 months or > 1.0 cm in 1 year).
3. Any symptomatic aneurysm (e.g., back pain, abdominal pain) regardless of size.

cards.q: Compare the hemodynamics of Hypovolemic vs. Cardiogenic shock.
cards.a:
• Hypovolemic Shock: Decreased Cardiac Output (CO), Decreased Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP), Increased Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR), Decreased Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation (\(S_vO_2\)).
• Cardiogenic Shock: Decreased CO, Increased PCWP (preload accumulates behind failing LV), Increased SVR, Decreased \(S_vO_2\).

cards.q: Compare the hemodynamics of Distributive (Septic) vs. Obstructive shock.
cards.a:
• Septic Shock: Increased CO (hyperdynamic phase), Decreased PCWP, Decreased SVR (severe peripheral vasodilation), Increased \(S_vO_2\) (tissues cannot extract oxygen due to shunting).
• Obstructive Shock (e.g., PE, Tamponade): Decreased CO, Variable PCWP (increased in tamponade, decreased in PE), Increased SVR, Decreased \(S_vO_2\).

cards.q: What is the first-line vasopressor of choice for patients in Septic Shock unresponsive to fluid resuscitation?
cards.a: Norepinephrine (acts primarily as an \(\alpha_1\) agonist to cause vasoconstriction, with mild \(\beta_1\) agonist activity to maintain cardiac output).

cards.q: A patient with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) receives aspirin, nitroglycerin, and O<sub>2</sub>. What is the most critical next step in determining the revascularization pathway?
cards.a: Obtaining an immediate 12-lead ECG to differentiate STEMI from NSTEMI/Unstable Angina.

cards.q: What is the next best step in management for a patient with a STEMI presenting to a non-PCI capable hospital if transfer to a PCI center will take > 120 minutes?
cards.a: Administer fibrinolytic therapy (e.g., Alteplase, Tenecteplase) immediately if there are no contraindications, within 30 minutes of arrival.

cards.q: Which specific beta-blockers are proven to reduce mortality in patients with Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)?
cards.a: Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, and sustained-release Metoprolol succinate.

cards.q: A patient with HFrEF and an ejection fraction of 25% continues to have symptomatic heart failure despite optimal medical therapy with an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. What new medication should replace the ACE inhibitor?
cards.a: An ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor) such as Sacubitril/Valsartan.

cards.q: What is the primary indication for adding Ivabradine to the regimen of a patient with HFrEF?
cards.a: Symptomatic HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 35%) with a resting sinus heart rate ≥ 70 bpm despite maximum tolerated doses of beta-blockers.

cards.q: A patient with an inferior wall STEMI develops profound hypotension after receiving sublingual nitroglycerin. What is the most likely diagnosis and next best step?
cards.a: Right Ventricular (RV) infarction; administer intravenous fluids to maintain adequate right ventricular preload and avoid further nitrates/diuretics.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG finding associated with Digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Downsloping ST segment depression (the 'scooped' ST segment), though true toxicity often presents with premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) or atrial tachycardia with variable AV block.

cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome and develops atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. What medications are strongly contraindicated?
cards.a: AV nodal blocking agents (Beta-blockers, Calcium channel blockers, Digoxin, Adenosine) as they can promote conduction down the accessory pathway leading to ventricular fibrillation.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial treatment for a hemodynamically stable patient with WPW syndrome who develops atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response?
cards.a: Intravenous Procainamide or Ibutilide (or synchronized cardioversion if they become unstable).

cards.q: What is the initial management for a patient presenting with acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary edema, and a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg?
cards.a: Intravenous loop diuretics (e.g., Furosemide). Vasodilators (nitrates) should be avoided due to borderline hypotension.

cards.q: What murmur is characterized by an early decrescendo diastolic murmur best heard along the left sternal border, often associated with a widened pulse pressure and bounding pulses?
cards.a: Aortic Regurgitation (Insufficiency).

cards.q: What physical exam maneuver distinguishes the systolic murmur of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) from that of Aortic Stenosis (AS)?
cards.a: Valsalva maneuver or standing decreases venous return (preload). This increases the intensity of the HCM murmur but decreases the intensity of the AS murmur.

cards.q: What is the definitive, potentially curative therapy for symptomatic Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) refractory to medical management (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs)?
cards.a: Surgical myomectomy or alcohol septal ablation.

cards.q: A patient is found to have a bicuspid aortic valve on echocardiography. What other vascular abnormality should the patient be screened for?
cards.a: Aortic aneurysm (ascending aorta) and aortic coarctation.

cards.q: A patient presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves with leaning forward. ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression. What is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: NSAIDs (e.g., Ibuprofen) combined with Colchicine for acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis.

cards.q: A patient develops a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and a step-up in oxygen saturation from the right atrium to the right ventricle 3-5 days post-MI. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) secondary to myocardial rupture (typically LAD or RCA occlusion).

cards.q: A patient presents with sudden-onset hypotension, elevated JVP, and clear lungs 3-5 days post-MI. What is the likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Free wall rupture leading to cardiac tamponade (typically LAD occlusion).

cards.q: A patient develops acute, severe pulmonary edema and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla 3-5 days post-MI. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Papillary muscle rupture leading to acute severe mitral regurgitation (typically RCA occlusion affecting the posteromedial papillary muscle).

cards.q: What is the most accurate diagnostic test for peripheral artery disease (PAD) in a patient with an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) of 1.35?
cards.a: Toe-Brachial Index (TBI). An ABI > 1.30 indicates calcified/incompressible vessels, rendering ABI falsely elevated, so TBI is needed.

cards.q: A 65-year-old male with a history of smoking undergoes an abdominal ultrasound which reveals a 4.5 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). What is the appropriate follow-up?
cards.a: Repeat ultrasound in 6 months (AAAs between 4.0 - 4.9 cm require ultrasound every 6-12 months). Repair is indicated if ≥ 5.5 cm or growing > 0.5 cm in 6 months.

cards.q: A patient presents with severe, tearing chest pain radiating to the back. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. What is the best initial diagnostic test if the patient has renal failure (Cr = 2.8)?
cards.a: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or non-contrast MRI (though TEE is preferred for definitive rapid diagnosis without contrast). CT Angiography requires IV contrast which is contraindicated in severe acute renal failure.

cards.q: What is the targeted blood pressure and heart rate for a patient with an acute aortic dissection?
cards.a: Systolic BP 100-120 mmHg and heart rate 60 bpm. Use IV beta-blockers (e.g., Labetalol, Esmolol) first to avoid reflex tachycardia, then Nitroprusside if needed.

cards.q: What is the characteristic change in the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) in a patient with cardiogenic shock vs. hypovolemic shock?
cards.a: PCWP is elevated in cardiogenic shock (due to left-sided heart failure backing up) and decreased in hypovolemic shock.

cards.q: Which physical exam finding is the most specific for diagnosing left-sided heart failure in a patient presenting with dyspnea?
cards.a: An S<sub>3</sub> gallop (ventricular gallop).

cards.q: What class of antihypertensive medications is most strongly associated with peripheral edema as a side effect?
cards.a: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., Amlodipine, Nifedipine).

cards.q: A patient with a history of asthma and hypertension presents with new-onset fatigue and heart rate of 52 bpm. He recently started a new antihypertensive medication. Which drug is most likely responsible?
cards.a: A non-selective beta-blocker (e.g., Propranolol) or a cardioselective one at high doses (e.g., Metoprolol, Atenolol) causing bradycardia.

cards.q: What is the recommended initial management for a patient in Monomorphic Ventricular Tachycardia who is hemodynamically stable?
cards.a: Intravenous Amiodarone (preferred) or Procainamide.

cards.q: What is the recommended therapy for Torsades de Pointes in a hemodynamically stable patient?
cards.a: Intravenous Magnesium Sulfate. If unstable, perform immediate defibrillation.

cards.q: A patient with new-onset Atrial Fibrillation of 3 days duration is hemodynamically stable and requires cardioversion. What must be done prior to cardioversion?
cards.a: A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) to rule out a left atrial appendage thrombus, OR 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation.

cards.q: What is the CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score threshold at which chronic oral anticoagulation is strongly recommended for a patient with non-valvular Atrial Fibrillation?
cards.a: A score of ≥ 2 in men or ≥ 3 in women.

cards.q: A patient presenting with acute peripheral arterial occlusion (acute limb ischemia) has a pulseless, cold, and pale leg but intact motor and sensory function. What is the immediate next step in management?
cards.a: Start intravenous Heparin immediately, followed by emergent surgical evaluation for revascularization.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnosis method for cardiac amyloidosis presenting as restrictive cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Endomyocardial biopsy showing apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain under polarized light (though bone scintigraphy (Tc-PYP) is often used first for ATTR amyloidosis).

cards.q: A patient with a history of breast cancer treated with radiation presents with elevated JVP, Kussmaul's sign, and a pericardial knock on auscultation. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Constrictive Pericarditis.

cards.q: What is Kussmaul's sign and what does it indicate?
cards.a: A paradoxical rise (or lack of fall) in the jugular venous pressure (JVP) with inspiration. It indicates impaired right ventricular filling (e.g., constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, RV infarction).

cards.q: What is the typical presentation and ECG finding for a patient with an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)?
cards.a: Fixed splitting of the S<sub>2</sub> sound and an incomplete right bundle branch block (RBBB) pattern on ECG.

cards.q: A patient with a mechanical aortic valve requires anticoagulation. What is the anticoagulant of choice and the target INR?
cards.a: Warfarin. Target INR is 2.0 - 3.0 for a mechanical aortic valve without risk factors (2.5 - 3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve or aortic valve with additional risk factors).

cards.q: In a patient presenting with hypertensive emergency and acute pulmonary edema, what is the best initial antihypertensive medication?
cards.a: Intravenous Nitroglycerin or Nitroprusside (with loop diuretics). Avoid beta-blockers as they decrease contractility.

cards.q: In a patient presenting with hypertensive emergency and acute ischemic stroke, what is the blood pressure threshold to treat if they are NOT receiving thrombolytics?
cards.a: Treat only if BP is > 220/120 mmHg. If they ARE receiving thrombolytics (tPA), keep BP < 185/110 mmHg prior to tPA and < 180/105 mmHg after.

cards.q: A young patient with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis most likely has what condition?
cards.a: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). Check plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR > 20 is suggestive).

cards.q: A patient develops a dry, hacking cough after starting a new medication for hypertension. What is the mechanism of this side effect?
cards.a: Accumulation of bradykinin due to Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibition.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in a patient with a prior history of a massive myocardial infarction and a low ejection fraction?
cards.a: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) or Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) degenerating from an arrhythmogenic scar.

cards.q: Which antiarrhythmic drug class is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease (e.g., prior MI, heart failure) due to an increased risk of proarrhythmia?
cards.a: Class IC antiarrhythmics (e.g., Flecainide, Propafenone).

cards.q: A patient presents with syncope and an ECG shows a PR interval of 0.28 seconds and grouped beating with a progressively lengthening PR interval before a dropped QRS complex. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Second-degree AV Block, Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach).

cards.q: A patient with syncope has an ECG showing constant PR intervals followed by intermittent dropped QRS complexes. What is the diagnosis and best management?
cards.a: Second-degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II. Management is permanent pacemaker insertion as it often progresses to complete heart block.

cards.q: What lipid-lowering medication is indicated for patients with clinical ASCVD (e.g., prior MI, stroke) regardless of baseline LDL levels?
cards.a: A high-intensity statin (e.g., Atorvastatin 40-80 mg or Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg).

cards.q: A patient on a statin develops muscle pain and dark urine. Creatine kinase is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis and next best step?
cards.a: Statin-induced rhabdomyolysis. Discontinue the statin immediately and start aggressive intravenous fluid hydration to prevent acute tubular necrosis.

cards.q: What is the triad of Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusive disease)?
cards.a: 1) Bilateral hip, thigh, and buttock claudication, 2) Absent or diminished femoral pulses, and 3) Erectile dysfunction.

cards.q: A patient post-cardiac catheterization develops a pulsatile mass with a systolic bruit at the femoral puncture site. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm. Diagnose with duplex ultrasound.

cards.q: A patient with Marfan syndrome presents with a high-pitched blowing early diastolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border. What is the underlying pathology?
cards.a: Aortic root dilation leading to Aortic Regurgitation.

cards.q: A patient taking Amiodarone chronically should have what routine screening tests performed to monitor for toxicities?
cards.a: Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4), Liver function tests (LFTs), and Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) / Chest X-ray.

cards.q: What is the formula for Cardiac Output (CO) using Stroke Volume (SV) and Heart Rate (HR), and how is Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) calculated from SBP and DBP?
cards.a:
CO = SV × HR
MAP = DBP + ⅓(SBP - DBP) = (2 × DBP + SBP) / 3

cards.q: What is the single most effective intervention to decrease mortality in a patient presenting with acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) within 12 hours of symptom onset?
cards.a: Immediate percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 90 minutes of door-to-balloon time (or fibrinolytic therapy within 120 minutes if PCI is unavailable).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of symptoms for severe aortic stenosis, and what is the definitive management once symptomatic?
cards.a:
Triad: SAD (Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea).
Definitive treatment: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement (SAVR) or TAVR.

cards.q: Which classes of medications are proven to improve long-term mortality in patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF, EF ≤ 40%)?
cards.a: ACEi/ARB/ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan), Beta-blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), MRAs (spironolactone/eplerenone), and SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin).

cards.q: In a patient with acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema without hypotension, what is the initial medical management?
cards.a: IV loop diuretics (e.g., Furosemide) + IV vasodilators (e.g., Nitroglycerin) to rapidly decrease cardiac preload and capillary wedge pressure, alongside supplemental O2.

cards.q: What is the initial empiric antibiotic therapy for acute native valve infective endocarditis in an IV drug user or critically ill patient?
cards.a: IV Vancomycin (covering MRSA) plus IV Cefepime or Gentamicin (covering Gram-negative bacilli and Enterococcus).

cards.q: What is Beck's triad for cardiac tamponade, and what are the characteristic ECG findings and pulsus paradoxus definition?
cards.a:
Beck's triad: Hypotension, JVD, Muffled heart sounds.
ECG: Electrical alternans.
Pulsus paradoxus: > 10 mmHg drop in SBP during inspiration.

cards.q: What is the immediate first-line pharmacological agent used to lower blood pressure and dP/dt in acute aortic dissection?
cards.a: IV Esmolol or Labetalol (IV beta-blockers) to target HR < 60/min and SBP 100–120 mmHg before initiating vasodilators.

cards.q: How is the decision to start long-term anticoagulation made in a patient with non-valvular Atrial Fibrillation?
cards.a: Calculate the CHA2DS2-VASc score. A score ≥ 2 in men or ≥ 3 in women warrants oral anticoagulation (DOACs like apixaban or rivaroxaban preferred over warfarin).

cards.q: How do physical examination maneuvers affect the systolic murmur of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)?
cards.a: Murmur increases with decreased LV volume (e.g., Valsalva strain, standing). Murmur decreases with increased LV volume/afterload (e.g., squatting, handgrip, passive leg raise).

cards.q: What is the step-by-step emergency management for severe hyperkalemia ([K+] > 6.5 mEq/L) with ECG changes?
cards.a:
1. Calcium gluconate (membrane stabilization)
2. Insulin + IV Dextrose and/or Albuterol (intracellular shift)
3. Loop diuretics / Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate / Hemodialysis (elimination).

cards.q: What defines a hypertensive emergency versus hypertensive urgency, and what is the target blood pressure reduction rate?
cards.a:
Emergency = SBP > 180 mmHg or DBP > 120 mmHg WITH acute end-organ damage.
Target: Reduce Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) by 10–20% in the 1st hour, then another 5–15% over 23 hours.

cards.q: What are the typical pulmonary artery catheter hemodynamic findings in cardiogenic shock (CO/CI, PCWP, SVR)?
cards.a:
Cardiac Output (CO): ↓
Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP): ↑
Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR): ↑

cards.q: What is the initial dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) regimen for a patient presenting with Unstable Angina / NSTEMI?
cards.a: Aspirin (162–325 mg initial loading dose) plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., Ticagrelor, Prasugrel, or Clopidogrel) for at least 12 months.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic ECG finding for 3rd-degree (complete) AV block, and what is the definitive treatment?
cards.a:
Finding: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes (regular P-P and R-R intervals with variable PR intervals).
Definitive treatment: Permanent pacemaker placement.

cards.q: What is the immediate first-line intravenous treatment for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia known as Torsades de Pointes?
cards.a: IV Magnesium Sulfate (2 g IV bolus).

cards.q: What is the initial diagnostic test for suspected Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD), and what value indicates ischemia?
cards.a:
Diagnostic test: Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI).
Value: ABI ≤ 0.90 is diagnostic of PAD; ABI < 0.40 indicates severe limb-threatening ischemia.

cards.q: What physical exam murmur is characteristic of acute or chronic severe mitral regurgitation, and where does it radiate?
cards.a: Holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur best heard at the cardiac apex (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line) radiating to the axilla.

cards.q: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test for a patient with suspected stable angina who has a normal baseline ECG and can exercise?
cards.a: Exercise ECG stress testing (treadmill stress test).

cards.q: What is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, where is it typically located, and what classic physical exam finding is associated with it?
cards.a: Atrial Myxoma (80% in the left atrium). Classic finding: Mid-diastolic 'tumor plop' murmur simulating mitral stenosis, accompanied by positional syncopal episodes.

cards.q: What is the criteria for diagnosing COPD on spirometry?
cards.a:
A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70.
Note: In contrast to asthma, this airflow obstruction is typically not fully reversible.

cards.q: What long-term therapies are proven to reduce mortality in COPD patients with chronic hypoxemia?
cards.a:
Long-term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT) for ≥ 15 hours/day.

Indications:
1. Resting \(P_aO_2\) ≤ 55 mmHg or \(S_aO_2\) ≤ 88%.
2. Resting \(P_aO_2\) 56–59 mmHg with signs of cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, or erythrocytosis (hematocrit > 55%).

cards.q: What is the management of a patient presenting with an acute COPD exacerbation?
cards.a:
1. Oxygen: Target saturation of 88–92% to avoid hypercapnia and respiratory drive suppression.
2. Bronchodilators: Inhaled short-acting beta-agonists (SABA, e.g., albuterol) + short-acting anticholinergics (SAMA, e.g., ipratropium).
3. Systemic Glucocorticoids: Oral prednisone or IV methylprednisolone (usually 5-day course).
4. Antibiotics: (e.g., macrolide, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolone) if the patient has increased sputum volume, increased purulence, and/or increased dyspnea.

cards.q: What is the stepwise approach to chronic asthma management?
cards.a:
• Step 1: As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred) or SABA.
• Step 2: Daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) + PRN SABA, or as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol.
• Step 3: Low-dose ICS + Long-acting beta-agonist (LABA).
• Step 4: Medium-dose ICS + LABA.
• Step 5: High-dose ICS + LABA + consider phenotypic add-on therapies (e.g., LAMA, anti-IgE omalizumab).

cards.q: What is the Samter Triad (Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease, AERD)?
cards.a:
1. Asthma
2. Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
3. Aspirin/NSAID hypersensitivity (due to leukotriene overproduction).

cards.q: List the components of the Wells Criteria for Pulmonary Embolism (PE) and their point values.
cards.a:
• 3.0 pts: Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT; PE is the #1 diagnosis or equally likely.
• 1.5 pts: HR > 100 bpm; Immobilization (≥ 3 days) or surgery within last 4 weeks; Previous DVT/PE.
• 1.0 pt: Hemoptysis; Malignancy (active or treated within 6 months).

cards.q: Outline the diagnostic algorithm for suspected PE based on Wells score.
cards.a:
• Wells Score ≤ 4 (PE Unlikely): Perform a high-sensitivity D-Dimer. If normal, PE is excluded. If elevated, proceed to CTPA.
• Wells Score > 4 (PE Likely): Bypass D-dimer and proceed directly to CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) (or V/Q scan if CTPA is contraindicated, e.g., in severe renal impairment or contrast allergy).

cards.q: What is the management of a hemodynamically unstable (hypotensive) patient with a confirmed or highly suspected PE?
cards.a: Immediate systemic thrombolytic therapy (e.g., alteplase) or catheter-directed embolectomy if thrombolysis is contraindicated.

cards.q: Define Light's Criteria for pleural fluid analysis.
cards.a:
A pleural effusion is classified as exudative if at least one of the following is met:
1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein ratio > 0.5.
2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH ratio > 0.6.
3. Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal for serum LDH.
Note: If none are met, the fluid is transudative.

cards.q: Compare common etiologies of Transudative vs. Exudative pleural effusions.
cards.a:
• Transudative: Heart Failure (most common), Cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax), Nephrotic syndrome (due to low oncotic pressure).
• Exudative: Parapneumonic effusion/pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary infarction/PE, autoimmune diseases (SLE, RA), uremic pleuritis.

cards.q: What pleural fluid findings define a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema?
cards.a:
• Pleural fluid pH < 7.2.
• Pleural fluid glucose < 60 mg/dL.
• Pleural fluid LDH > 1,000 U/L.
• Presence of bacteria on Gram stain/culture or gross pus.
Management: Requires chest tube drainage in addition to IV antibiotics.

cards.q: What is the CURB-65 scoring system for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) disposition?
cards.a:
• C: Confusion (new)
• U: Urea > 19 mg/dL (BUN > 20 mg/dL)
• R: Respiratory Rate ≥ 30/min
• B: Blood Pressure (Systolic < 90 or Diastolic ≤ 60 mmHg)
• 65: Age ≥ 65 years

Disposition:
• 0–1 points: Outpatient management.
• 2 points: Inpatient (ward) admission.
• ≥ 3 points: Consider ICU admission.

cards.q: What is the empiric outpatient treatment for CAP in a healthy patient with no comorbidities?
cards.a:
• Amoxicillin (high dose) OR
• Doxycycline OR
• Macrolide (Azithromycin/Clarithromycin, only if local pneumococcal resistance is < 25%).

cards.q: What is the empiric outpatient treatment for CAP in a patient with significant comorbidities (e.g., CKD, DM, HF, COPD)?
cards.a:
• Respiratory Fluoroquinolone monotherapy (e.g., Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin) OR
• Beta-lactam (e.g., Amoxicillin-clavulanate, Cefuroxime) + Macrolide or Doxycycline.

cards.q: What is the empiric inpatient (non-ICU) treatment for CAP?
cards.a:
• IV Beta-lactam (e.g., Ceftriaxone, Ampicillin-sulbactam) + IV Macrolide (e.g., Azithromycin) OR
• Monotherapy with an IV Respiratory Fluoroquinolone (e.g., Levofloxacin).

cards.q: Define Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) and state the key pathogens to cover empirically.
cards.a:
Pneumonia occurring ≥ 48 hours after hospital admission.

Pathogens & Treatment: Must cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa and MRSA. Empiric regimen includes an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Piperacillin-tazobactam, Cefepime) + Vancomycin or Linezolid.

cards.q: What diagnostic criteria define Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)?
cards.a:
1. Acute onset (within 1 week of a known clinical insult).
2. Bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by pleural effusions, collapse, or nodules.
3. Respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload (objective exclusion via echocardiogram if no risk factor present).
4. Severe hypoxemia: \(P_aO_2/F_iO_2\) ratio ≤ 300 mmHg with PEEP ≥ 5 \(cmH_2O\).

cards.q: What mechanical ventilation settings are proven to reduce mortality in patients with ARDS?
cards.a:
• Low tidal volume ventilation: 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight (prevents barotrauma/volutrauma).
• Permissive hypercapnia: Allowing elevated \(P_aCO_2\) to maintain low tidal volumes, keeping plateau pressure < 30 \(cmH_2O\).
• High PEEP: To recruit alveoli and improve oxygenation.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and diagnostic biopsy finding of Sarcoidosis.
cards.a:
• Clinical: Young African American female, dry cough, dyspnea, erythema nodosum, uveitis, lupus pernio.
• Imaging: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR.
• Labs: Elevated serum ACE, hypercalcemia / hypercalciuria (due to 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granulomas producing active Vitamin D).
• Biopsy: Non-caseating granulomas.

cards.q: What are the spirometry and lung volume findings in restrictive lung disease?
cards.a:
• FEV1/FVC ratio: Normal or increased (> 70–80%).
• TLC (Total Lung Capacity): Decreased (< 80% predicted).
• RV (Residual Volume) & FVC: Decreased.

cards.q: Describe the imaging features and clinical course of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF).
cards.a:
• HRCT Chest: Peripheral, subpleural reticular opacities with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis.
• Clinical: Progressive exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough in older adults; bibasilar inspiratory Velcro-like crackles; digital clubbing.

cards.q: Contrast Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) and Central Sleep Apnea (CSA) by pathogenesis and diagnosis.
cards.a:
• OSA: Physical collapse of the upper airway (pharyngeal tissues) during sleep despite ongoing respiratory effort. Strongly associated with obesity.
• CSA: Temporary loss of respiratory drive from the brainstem (CNS dysfunction) with absent respiratory effort. Associated with heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes breathing), opioid use, and stroke.
• Diagnosis: Polysomnography showing Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) ≥ 5/hour.

cards.q: What is the initial diagnostic test for a patient suspected of having OSA?
cards.a: Polysomnography (in-lab sleep study) or home sleep apnea testing.

cards.q: What is the management algorithm for a solitary pulmonary nodule (< 3 cm) detected on chest X-ray?
cards.a:
1. Compare with prior chest imaging to assess stability.
2. If no prior imaging, perform a high-resolution chest CT.
3. Management is based on risk factors (size, edge characteristics, patient smoking history):
• Low risk/small (< 6 mm): No follow-up or routine CT scan in 12 months.
• Intermediate risk/growing: Biopsy (bronchoscopy or CT-guided FNA) or PET scan.
• High risk (> 2 cm, spiculates, elderly smoker): Surgical resection.

cards.q: How does a tension pneumothorax cause hemodynamic collapse?
cards.a: One-way valve allows air to enter the pleural space but not exit. The accumulating intrapleural pressure shifts the mediastinum to the contralateral side, compressing the superior and inferior vena cava, which reduces venous return (preload) to the heart and causes obstructive shock.

cards.q: What is the immediate emergency management of a tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Needle decompression with a large-bore needle in the 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line (or 4th/5th intercostal space at the anterior/midaxillary line), followed immediately by chest tube thoracostomy.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of a small (< 2 cm) primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea in a tall, thin male smoker.
• Management: Observation and supplemental oxygen (promotes nitrogen resorption from the pleural space).

cards.q: Define Bronchiectasis and its classic clinical presentation.
cards.a:
Permanent, abnormal dilation and destruction of major bronchi due to chronic infection and inflammation.

Key Presentation: Copious, purulent, foul-smelling sputum production; recurrent respiratory infections; hemoptysis.
Imaging: High-resolution CT showing tram-track sign and signet-ring sign.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect and clinical presentation of Kartagener Syndrome?
cards.a:
Autosomal recessive mutation causing a defect in the dynein arms of cilia (primary ciliary dyskinesia).

Triad:
1. Situs inversus
2. Chronic sinusitis/nasal polyps
3. Bronchiectasis
Associated with: Male infertility (immotile sperm).

cards.q: Which occupational lung disease is associated with shipyards, construction, and insulation work, and increases the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma?
cards.a:
Asbestosis.

Key Feature: CXR shows pleural plaques (calcified plaques on the diaphragm) and interstitial fibrosis in the lower lobes. Asbestos bodies (ferruginous bodies) on histology. Bronchogenic carcinoma is more common than mesothelioma in these patients.

cards.q: Which occupational lung disease is associated with sandblasting, mining, and stonecutting, and predisposes patients to tuberculosis?
cards.a:
Silicosis.

Key Feature: CXR shows nodular opacities in the upper lobes with eggshell calcifications of the hilar lymph nodes. Silica impairs macrophage phagolysosome formation, increasing susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

cards.q: Which occupational lung disease is associated with aerospace, electronics, and manufacturing industries, and presents similarly to sarcoidosis with non-caseating granulomas?
cards.a: Berylliosis. Diagnosed with a positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and laboratory findings of Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, coma. Cherry-red skin color (rare, post-mortem).
• Labs: Normal \(P_aO_2\) on ABG, but severely reduced oxygen saturation on co-oximetry. Elevated carboxyhemoglobin level.
• Treatment: 100% normobaric oxygen (competes with CO binding to hemoglobin) or hyperbaric oxygen in severe cases.

cards.q: What is Methemoglobinemia, and what is the treatment of choice?
cards.a:
Oxidation of iron in hemoglobin from ferrous (\(Fe^{2+}\)) to ferric (\(Fe^{3+}\)) state, which cannot bind oxygen. Caused by local anesthetics (benzocaine), dapsone, and nitrites.

Presentation: Cyanosis, chocolate-colored blood, normal \(P_aO_2\), but low oxygen saturation.
Treatment: IV Methylene Blue.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic gold standard for confirming Pulmonary Hypertension?
cards.a: Right heart catheterization demonstrating a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg at rest.

cards.q: What ECG findings are associated with severe cor pulmonale / pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy (large R wave in V1), right axis deviation, right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale: tall, peaked P waves in lead II), and RBBB.

cards.q: What is the initial diagnostic test for a patient suspected of having a pleural effusion?
cards.a: Chest X-ray (upright PA and lateral). Pleural effusions present as blunting of the costophrenic angle.

cards.q: What is the utility of lateral decubitus chest X-rays in the evaluation of a pleural effusion?
cards.a: Assesses if the effusion is free-flowing or loculated, and determines if there is sufficient fluid volume (≥ 1 cm thick layer) to safely perform thoracentesis.

cards.q: What is the definition of a massive hemoptysis, and what is the immediate management priority?
cards.a:
• Definition: Expectoration of > 100–600 mL of blood in 24 hours.
• Priority: Airway protection. Place the patient in the lateral decubitus position with the bleeding lung down (prevents blood from aspirating into the healthy lung) and secure the airway via intubation, followed by bronchoscopy.

cards.q: Explain the classic clinical presentation of a pulmonary embolism.
cards.a: Sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxemia. Hemoptysis and low-grade fever may also be present.

cards.q: What ECG sign is highly specific (though insensitive) for right ventricular strain due to a massive PE?
cards.a: The S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S wave in lead I, Q wave in lead III, inverted T wave in lead III).

cards.q: What are the contraindications to systemic thrombolytic therapy in a patient with a massive PE?
cards.a: Active internal bleeding, recent intracranial or spinal surgery/trauma (within 2 months), history of hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke within 3 months, or intracranial neoplasm.

cards.q: What is the preferred treatment for a pregnant patient with a confirmed DVT or PE?
cards.a: Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) (e.g., enoxaparin). LMWH does not cross the placenta, unlike warfarin which is teratogenic.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient with a PE who has an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation?
cards.a: Placement of an Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) filter.

cards.q: What is the definition of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian Syndrome)?
cards.a: • Daytime hypercapnia (\(P_aCO_2\) ≥ 45 mmHg) in an obese patient (BMI ≥ 30 \(kg/m^2\)) that is not explained by another pulmonary disease.

cards.q: Which pneumonia pathogen is classically associated with hyponatremia, diarrhea, high fever, and neurologic symptoms, often spread via contaminated water systems?
cards.a:
Legionella pneumophila.

Diagnosis: Urine antigen test or PCR. Treatment: Macrolides (azithromycin) or Respiratory Fluoroquinolones.

cards.q: Which pneumonia pathogen is classically associated with bullous myringitis, cold agglutinins, and interstitial infiltrates in young adults?
cards.a: Mycoplasma pneumoniae ('walking pneumonia'). Treatment: Macrolides or Doxycycline (beta-lactams are ineffective because Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall).

cards.q: Which pneumonia pathogen is classically associated with current-jelly sputum in alcoholic or diabetic patients?
cards.a: Klebsiella pneumoniae. Often causes cavitary lesions in the upper lobes.

cards.q: What is the primary diagnostic test of choice to confirm suspected Active Tuberculosis?
cards.a: Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture (three morning sputum samples), along with nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT).

cards.q: What are the target blood gas parameters in a patient with chronic respiratory acidosis (e.g., severe COPD)?
cards.a: Elevated \(P_aCO_2\) with a near-normal pH due to renal compensation (metabolic alkalosis with elevated bicarbonate, \(HCO_3^-\)).

cards.q: What are the two interventions proven to reduce mortality in COPD?
cards.a: Smoking cessation and long-term supplemental O<sub>2</sub> therapy (if PaO<sub>2</sub> ≤ 55 mmHg or SaO<sub>2</sub> ≤ 88%, or PaO<sub>2</sub> ≤ 59 with cor pulmonale/polycythemia).

cards.q: What is the classic spirometry finding in obstructive lung diseases (Asthma/COPD)?
cards.a: Decreased FEV<sub>1</sub>, decreased FVC, and an FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC ratio < 0.70.

cards.q: How do you differentiate asthma from COPD on pulmonary function testing?
cards.a: Asthma shows reversibility: an increase in FEV<sub>1</sub> by ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL after bronchodilator administration.

cards.q: What is the initial medical management for an acute COPD exacerbation?
cards.a: Short-acting bronchodilators (albuterol + ipratropium), systemic corticosteroids (e.g., oral prednisone for 5 days), and antibiotics (if ≥ 2 cardinal symptoms: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, increased sputum purulence).

cards.q: Which non-invasive ventilation method is indicated for a severe COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35 and PaCO<sub>2</sub> > 45 mmHg)?
cards.a: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NPPV), such as BiPAP.

cards.q: What are the components of Light's criteria used to identify an exudative pleural effusion?
cards.a: Pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5, Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH > 0.6, or Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal for serum LDH (any one = exudative).

cards.q: What type of pleural effusion is classically caused by congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome?
cards.a: Transudative effusion (driven by altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressure).

cards.q: A patient presents with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Pulmonary Embolism (PE).

cards.q: In a patient with high clinical suspicion for PE (high Wells score), what is the first step in management before diagnostic imaging?
cards.a: Start empiric anticoagulation (e.g., LMWH or unfractionated heparin) if there are no contraindications.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic imaging test of choice for a suspected PE in a patient with a normal baseline chest X-ray and normal renal function?
cards.a: CT pulmonary angiography (CTA).

cards.q: Which imaging modality is preferred to diagnose a PE in a patient with chronic kidney disease (GFR < 30) or severe contrast allergy?
cards.a: Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) scan.

cards.q: What is the classic, though rare, ECG finding in pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: S<sub>1</sub>Q<sub>3</sub>T<sub>3</sub> pattern (deep S in lead I, Q wave and inverted T in lead III). The most common finding is sinus tachycardia.

cards.q: What acid-base disturbance is typically seen initially in acute asthma exacerbation or pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Primary respiratory alkalosis (due to hyperventilation causing decreased PaCO<sub>2</sub>).

cards.q: In a patient with a severe asthma exacerbation, what does a normal or rising PaCO<sub>2</sub> indicate?
cards.a: Impending respiratory failure (muscle fatigue), requiring immediate ICU evaluation and possible intubation.

cards.q: What is the criteria for diagnosing Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) (Berlin definition)?
cards.a: Acute onset (within 1 week of insult), bilateral opacities on chest imaging, not fully explained by heart failure/fluid overload, and a PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> ratio ≤ 300 mmHg.

cards.q: What is the preferred ventilator management strategy in ARDS to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury?
cards.a: Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight) and adequate PEEP (to prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation).

cards.q: A 30-year-old African American female presents with dry cough, erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and hypercalcemia. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Sarcoidosis.

cards.q: What is the most definitive diagnostic test for sarcoidosis, and what is the classic histologic finding?
cards.a: Transbronchial or excisional biopsy; shows noncaseating granulomas.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Systemic corticosteroids.

cards.q: What occupational lung disease is seen in sandblasters, miners, and glassmakers, typically involving the upper lobes and demonstrating "eggshell calcifications" of hilar lymph nodes?
cards.a: Silicosis.

cards.q: Silicosis is associated with an increased risk of which infectious disease?
cards.a: Tuberculosis (due to impaired macrophage function).

cards.q: What occupational lung disease is seen in shipyard workers, plumbers, and roofers, typically involving the lower lobes and pleural plaques?
cards.a: Asbestosis.

cards.q: What is the most common malignancy associated with asbestos exposure?
cards.a: Bronchogenic carcinoma (more common than mesothelioma).

cards.q: A 45-year-old non-smoker presents with progressive dyspnea, fine bibasilar end-inspiratory crackles (Velcro-like), and clubbing. High-resolution CT shows honeycombing. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF).

cards.q: What are the primary treatments for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) to slow disease progression?
cards.a: Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone, nintedanib).

cards.q: What is the CURB-65 criteria used for, and what are its components?
cards.a: Used to determine hospitalization for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP). Confusion, Uremia (BUN > 19 mg/dL), Respiratory rate ≥ 30, Blood pressure (SBP < 90 or DBP ≤ 60), Age ≥ 65. Score 0-1: Outpatient, 2-3: Inpatient ward, 4-5: ICU.

cards.q: What is the empiric outpatient treatment for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) in a healthy patient with no comorbidities and no recent antibiotic use?
cards.a: Amoxicillin OR a macrolide (azithromycin) OR doxycycline.

cards.q: What is the empiric inpatient treatment for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) (non-ICU)?
cards.a: Respiratory fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin or levofloxacin) OR a beta-lactam (ceftriaxone) + a macrolide (azithromycin).

cards.q: What is the empiric antibiotic coverage for Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) or Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)?
cards.a: Coverage for MRSA (vancomycin or linezolid) and antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem).

cards.q: Which pneumonia-causing pathogen is associated with hyponatremia, diarrhea, confusion, and elevated transaminases, often linked to contaminated water sources?
cards.a: Legionella pneumophila.

cards.q: Which pathogen typically causes a "lobar" pneumonia with "rusty" colored sputum?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: Which pneumonia-causing pathogen is commonly seen in alcoholics and causes "currant jelly" sputum?
cards.a: Klebsiella pneumoniae.

cards.q: A patient from the Ohio/Mississippi River Valley presents with pneumonia after exploring caves (bat/bird droppings). Diagnosis?
cards.a: Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum).

cards.q: A patient from the Southwestern US presents with pneumonia, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Coccidioidomycosis (Coccidioides immitis).

cards.q: What is the classic chest X-ray finding in reactivation Tuberculosis?
cards.a: Apical cavitary lesion.

cards.q: What are the common adverse effects of Isoniazid (INH)?
cards.a: Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy (prevented by administering Vitamin B<sub>6</sub>/pyridoxine).

cards.q: Which TB medication causes red-orange discoloration of body fluids (urine, tears, sweat)?
cards.a: Rifampin.

cards.q: Which TB medication is associated with optic neuritis (decreased visual acuity, red-green color blindness)?
cards.a: Ethambutol.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of a solitary pulmonary nodule?
cards.a: Infectious granuloma (e.g., histoplasmosis, TB).

cards.q: What are the criteria for a benign-appearing solitary pulmonary nodule on CT?
cards.a: Smooth borders, size < 8 mm, and dense central, "popcorn," or concentric ("bullseye") calcifications.

cards.q: What is the recommended lung cancer screening guideline by the USPSTF?
cards.a: Annual low-dose chest CT for adults aged 50-80 with a ≥ 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.

cards.q: Which type of lung cancer is typically centrally located, associated with smoking, and causes hypercalcemia (via PTHrP)?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: Which type of lung cancer is the most common overall, typically peripherally located, and often seen in non-smokers?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which type of lung cancer is centrally located, highly aggressive, and associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like SIADH, ectopic ACTH (Cushing's), and Lambert-Eaton syndrome?
cards.a: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).

cards.q: A patient presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on one side of the face, along with right shoulder pain. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor) causing Horner syndrome.

cards.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic test for Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)?
cards.a: Nocturnal polysomnography (sleep study) showing ≥ 15 obstructive respiratory events/hour, or ≥ 5/hour with symptoms.

cards.q: A patient with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, steatorrhea, and failure to thrive presents for evaluation. A sweat chloride test is > 60 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Cystic Fibrosis.

cards.q: A young, non-smoking patient presents with COPD (emphysema) and liver cirrhosis. What is the underlying genetic defect?
cards.a: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency.

cards.q: A patient presents with copious, foul-smelling purulent sputum, recurrent respiratory infections, and hemoptysis. High-resolution CT shows dilated bronchi with "tram-track" markings. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Bronchiectasis.

cards.q: What is the initial test of choice for diagnosing Pulmonary Hypertension?
cards.a: Transthoracic echocardiogram (estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure); however, right heart catheterization is required for definitive diagnosis (mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg).

cards.q: What is the formula for the Alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient) and what does an elevated gradient (>15 mmHg) indicate?
cards.a: PAO2 - PaO2, where PAO2 = (FiO2 × (760 - 47)) - (PaCO2 / 0.8). An elevated gradient indicates hypoxemia due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion defect, or right-to-left shunt (vs. hypoventilation/low FiO2 where A-a gradient is normal).

cards.q: What are Light's criteria for distinguishing an exudative pleural effusion from a transudative pleural effusion?
cards.a:
An effusion is exudative if ≥1 of the following is present:
1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein > 0.5
2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH > 0.6
3. Pleural fluid LDH > 2⁄3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

cards.q: What are the key HRCT findings and microscopic pattern diagnostic of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)?
cards.a: High-resolution CT shows subpleural honeycombing, reticular opacities, and traction bronchiectasis, corresponding to a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern.

cards.q: What is the classic thoracic imaging finding and key histological feature of sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with parenchymal reticular infiltrates on CXR, and non-caseating granulomas on biopsy (associated with elevated ACE and hypercalcemia secondary to 1-α-hydroxylase activity).

cards.q: What is the first-line non-invasive ventilatory support for acute COPD exacerbation with persistent hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35, P<sub>a</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> > 45 mmHg)?
cards.a: Non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV/BiPAP). Intubation is indicated if NIPPV fails after 1-2 hours or if the patient has severe encephalopathy or hemodynamic instability.

cards.q: What is the preferred reliever and controller therapy for mild persistent asthma according to modern GINA guidelines?
cards.a: As-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-formoterol (combination ICS + long-acting β2-agonist) serves as both controller and quick reliever therapy.

cards.q: In a patient with suspected Pulmonary Embolism (PE), how does the Wells Score dictate initial diagnostic testing?
cards.a:
If Wells score is ≤ 4 (PE unlikely) → order high-sensitivity D-dimer test.
If Wells score is > 4 (PE likely) → order CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) directly.

cards.q: What is the management step for a high-risk solitary pulmonary nodule (>2 cm, spiculated borders, smoking history)?
cards.a: Surgical resection (or biopsy if intermediate risk or high surgical risk). If low risk (<0.8 cm, smooth, young non-smoker) → serial CT monitoring.

cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for ARDS and the target ventilation parameters to reduce mortality?
cards.a:
Criteria: Acute onset (≤1 wk), PaO2/FiO2 ratio ≤ 300 mmHg with PEEP ≥ 5 cm H2O, bilateral opacities not fully explained by heart failure.
Management: Low tidal volume (4-8 mL/kg ideal body weight) and high PEEP.

cards.q: How does Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) differ from isolated Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) on daytime arterial blood gas (ABG)?
cards.a: OHS presents with awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) and hypoxemia (PaO2 < 70 mmHg) with compensatory elevated serum HCO3-, whereas isolated OSA has normal daytime ABG values.

cards.q: Which underlying mechanism of arterial hypoxemia does NOT correct with 100% supplemental O2?
cards.a: Right-to-left shunt (e.g., intracardiac right-to-left shunts, pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, or complete alveolar filling/atelectasis).

cards.q: What radiologic features distinguish Silicosis from Asbestosis?
cards.a:
Silicosis: Nodular opacities in upper lobes with "eggshell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes.
Asbestosis: Interstitial fibrosis in lower lobes with pleural plaques (diaphragmatic calcifications).

cards.q: What are the primary differential diagnoses for a pleural effusion with a glucose level < 60 mg/dL?
cards.a: Complicated parapneumonic effusion / empyema, rheumatoid arthritis effusion (often < 30 mg/dL), tuberculosis, lupus pleuritis, and malignancy.

cards.q: What pleural fluid analysis parameters indicate a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring chest tube thoracostomy drainage?
cards.a: pH < 7.20, glucose < 60 mg/dL, LDH > 1000 U/L, or presence of frank pus / positive Gram stain / positive culture.

cards.q: In a young non-smoker (<45 years) presenting with emphysema and abnormal liver function tests, what is the underlying diagnosis and pulmonary disease distribution?
cards.a: α1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ genotype), causing panacinar emphysema predominantly affecting the lower lobes, along with liver cirrhosis.

cards.q: What pattern of pulmonary function testing (PFT) parameters is diagnostic of Restrictive Lung Disease?
cards.a: Decreased Total Lung Capacity (TLC < 80% predicted), decreased FVC, normal or elevated FEV1/FVC ratio (≥ 70%).

cards.q: On a mechanical ventilator, if Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP) is elevated but Plateau Pressure (Pplat) is normal, what is the underlying physiological issue?
cards.a: Increased airway resistance (e.g., bronchospasm, airway secretions, kinked endotracheal tube). If both PIP and Pplat are elevated, lung compliance is decreased (e.g., ARDS, pulmonary edema).

cards.q: What are the 5 components of the CURB-65 score for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) risk stratification?
cards.a:
Confusion, Urea > 19 mg/dL (7 mmol/L), Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min, Blood pressure (SBP < 90 or DBP ≤ 60 mmHg), Age ≥ 65.
(Score 0-1: Outpatient; Score 2: Inpatient ward; Score ≥ 3: Inpatient / ICU).

cards.q: How is Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) defined hemodynamically via Right Heart Catheterization?
cards.a: Mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg at rest, with normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP ≤ 15 mmHg) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR > 2 Wood units).

cards.q: How do Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning and Methemoglobinemia differ in terms of arterial blood gas (ABG) PaO2 and pulse oximetry (SpO2)?
cards.a:
Both have normal PaO2 on ABG.
CO poisoning shows falsely normal SpO2 (requires co-oximetry for HbCO).
Methemoglobinemia shows SpO2 fixed ~85% unresponsive to 100% O2.

cards.q: What is the Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG), and how do you interpret its values?
cards.a:
SAAG = (Serum Albumin) − (Ascitic Fluid Albumin).

Interpretation:
• SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL: Indicates portal hypertension (transudative process, e.g., Heart Failure, Cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome).
• SAAG < 1.1 g/dL: Indicates no portal hypertension (exudative process, e.g., Peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB, nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic criteria and treatment of choice for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
cards.a:
• Diagnosis: Ascitic fluid analysis showing absolute neutrophil (PMN) count ≥ 250 cells/mm\(^3\).
• Treatment: IV Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone. Add IV albumin (reduces risk of hepatorenal syndrome).
Prophylaxis: Oral fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) or TMP-SMX for patients with prior SBP, or low protein ascites (< 1.5 g/dL) + renal/hepatic impairment.

cards.q: Compare Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis (UC) by anatomical distribution and depth of inflammation.
cards.a:
• Crohn's Disease: Transmural inflammation; can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus (skip lesions). Terminal ileum is most commonly involved; rectal sparing.
• Ulcerative Colitis: Mucosal and submucosal inflammation only; limited to the colon and rectum, spreading continuously proximally from the rectum.

cards.q: Compare Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis (UC) by histology and endoscopy findings.
cards.a:
• Crohn's Disease: Non-caseating granulomas; cobblestone mucosa, aphthous ulcers, creeping fat, and strictures (string sign on barium swallow).
• Ulcerative Colitis: Crypt abscesses and architectural distortion; pseudopolyps, mucosal friability, and loss of haustra (lead-pipe colon).

cards.q: List the high-yield extraintestinal manifestations of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD).
cards.a:
• Both: Erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, episcleritis, uveitis, aphthous stomatitis, seronegative arthritis.
• Crohn's only: Nephrolithiasis (oxalate stones due to fat malabsorption binding calcium), gallstones.
• UC only: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) — strongly associated.

cards.q: Interpret the following Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive, HBeAg positive, anti-HBs negative.
cards.a:
Acute Hepatitis B infection (high infectivity).
• HBsAg = Active infection.
• anti-HBc IgM = Acute/recent infection.
• HBeAg = High viral replication/infectivity.

cards.q: Interpret the following Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc IgG positive, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc IgM negative.
cards.a:
Recovery/Immunity from natural infection.
• anti-HBs positive = Immunity.
• anti-HBc IgG positive = Exposed to natural virus (not vaccinated).

cards.q: Interpret the following Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs positive.
cards.a:
Immunity from Hepatitis B vaccination.
• anti-HBs positive = Immunity.
• anti-HBc negative = Never exposed to the core antigen (not exposed to natural virus).

cards.q: Interpret the following Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg positive for > 6 months, anti-HBc IgG positive, anti-HBs negative.
cards.a: Chronic Hepatitis B infection. HBsAg positivity persisting for > 6 months defines chronic infection.

cards.q: What is the definition of the Hepatitis B 'Window Period'?
cards.a: The time interval between the disappearance of HBsAg and the appearance of anti-HBs. During this time, the only diagnostic marker of acute infection may be anti-HBc IgM.

cards.q: What diagnostic criteria define Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a:
Requires ≥ 2 of the following:
1. Acute onset of severe, epigastric pain radiating to the back.
2. Lipase or Amylase levels ≥ 3 times the upper limit of normal.
3. Characteristic findings on abdominal imaging (CT abdomen with contrast or MRI).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis, and what is the initial imaging test of choice?
cards.a:
• Most common cause: Gallstones (followed closely by alcohol).
• Imaging of choice: Right upper quadrant ultrasound (to evaluate for gallstones/biliary tree dilation). CT abdomen is not required for diagnosis if clinical and lab criteria are met.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of initial medical management for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation (preferably with Lactated Ringer's) to prevent pancreatic necrosis, along with bowel rest and pain control.

cards.q: What is a pancreatic pseudocyst, and what is the management?
cards.a:
A fibrous wall (lacking epithelial lining) surrounding fluid, enzymes, and debris, occurring 4+ weeks after pancreatitis.

Management: Observation if asymptomatic and stable. Drainage (endoscopic or surgical) is indicated if symptomatic, infected, or expanding.

cards.q: Describe the screening and surveillance guidelines for Barrett's Esophagus.
cards.a:
• Screening: Screen patients with chronic GERD (> 5 years) + ≥ 2 risk factors (male, age > 50, white, obesity, smoking) using endoscopy with biopsy.
• Surveillance:
• No dysplasia: Endoscopy in 3–5 years.
• Low-grade dysplasia: Endoscopic ablation or surveillance in 6–12 months.
• High-grade dysplasia: Endoscopic mucosal resection or ablation.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation and diagnostic workup for Achalasia.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and weight loss.
• Barium Swallow: 'Bird's beak' deformity (tapering of the distal esophagus).
• Gold Standard: Esophageal Manometry showing incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and aperistalsis.

cards.q: What is Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES), and what are its diagnostic features?
cards.a:
Impaired inhibitory innervation leading to uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophageal body.

Presentation: Chest pain mimicking angina, dysphagia to solids/liquids.
Barium Swallow: 'Corkscrew' or 'rosary bead' esophagus.
Manometry: High-amplitude, simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions.

cards.q: Compare the clinical presentation of Gastric vs. Duodenal ulcers.
cards.a:
• Gastric Ulcers: Pain is worse with meals (food triggers acid release → irritation), leading to weight loss.
• Duodenal Ulcers: Pain is relieved by meals (food triggers bicarbonate-rich alkaline secretion in duodenum) and recurs 2–5 hours later; pain awake at night is common; weight gain.

cards.q: What is the preferred empiric triple and quadruple therapy for H. pylori eradication?
cards.a:
• Triple Therapy (only if local clarithromycin resistance is < 15%): PPI + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if penicillin-allergic).
• Quadruple Therapy (preferred/first-line due to resistance): PPI + Bismuth Subsalicylate + Metronidazole + Tetracycline.

cards.q: What is the screening and confirmatory test of choice for Celiac Disease?
cards.a:
• Screening: Serum IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) antibody + total serum IgA (to rule out IgA deficiency).
• Confirmatory: Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis.

cards.q: What is the pathogenesis and treatment of choice for Hepatic Encephalopathy?
cards.a:
Accumulation of neurotoxins (primarily ammonia, \(NH_3\)) due to hepatic dysfunction and portosystemic shunting.

Treatment: First-line is Lactulose (metabolized by gut bacteria to lactic acid, trapping ammonia as non-absorbable ammonium, \(NH_4^+\)), and Rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic that eliminates ammonia-producing gut bacteria).

cards.q: What is the first-line medication for the prevention (primary prophylaxis) of variceal bleeding in a patient with cirrhosis and medium/large esophageal varices?
cards.a: Non-selective beta-blockers (e.g., Nadolol or Propranolol) to reduce portal pressure by causing splanchnic vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What is the immediate management for a patient with acute variceal bleeding?
cards.a:
1. Hemodynamic stabilization (target hemoglobin 7–8 g/dL).
2. IV Octreotide (somatostatin analog that decreases splanchnic blood flow).
3. Prophylactic antibiotics (IV Ceftriaxone for ≤ 7 days, prevents SBP/infections).
4. Urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) for endoscopic band ligation.

cards.q: Compare Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) by site of damage, antibody association, and imaging findings.
cards.a:
• PBC: Autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts. Associated with Antimitochondrial Antibodies (AMA). Normal biliary tree on imaging.
• PSC: Inflammation/fibrosis of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts. Associated with p-ANCA and strongly linked to Ulcerative Colitis. MRCP/ERCP shows 'beaded' appearance (strictures and dilations).

cards.q: What are the classic manifestations, laboratory findings, and treatment of Hereditary Hemochromatosis?
cards.a:
• Manifestations: Hyperpigmentation ('bronze diabetes'), hepatomegaly/cirrhosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy/arrhythmias, pseudogout, hypogonadism.
• Labs: Elevated serum iron, elevated ferritin, transferrin saturation > 45% (often > 50-60%). HFE gene mutation (C282Y).
• Treatment: Therapeutic phlebotomy.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice and management for acute Diverticulitis?
cards.a:
• Diagnostic Test: CT Abdomen/Pelvis with contrast (shows colonic wall thickening, fat stranding).
• Treatment: Bowel rest, oral/IV antibiotics (ciprofloxacin + metronidazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate).
