cards.q: A patient with recurrent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia has elevated serum IgM but absent serum IgG, IgA, and IgE. What cell surface ligand interaction is defective?
cards.a: Defect in CD40 Ligand (CD40L / CD154) expressed on activated CD4+ T cells (Hyper-IgM Syndrome), which prevents interaction with CD40 on B cells, blocking class-switch recombination.

cards.q: Ten days after starting penicillin, a patient develops fever, urticarial rash, joint pain, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Lab tests show low serum C3 and C4 levels. What hypersensitivity type is responsible?
cards.a: Type III hypersensitivity (Serum Sickness), mediated by systemic immune complex (IgG-antigen) deposition that activates the classical complement cascade, lowering serum C3/C4.

cards.q: A patient on allopurinol develops fever, diffuse morbilliform eruption, facial swelling, peripheral eosinophilia (>1,500/μL), and elevated serum transaminases 4 weeks after drug initiation. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: DRESS Syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), a severe T-cell mediated drug reaction with multi-organ involvement (most commonly liver and kidney).

cards.q: What is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for long-term control of moderate-to-severe Allergic Rhinitis?
cards.a: Intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., fluticasone, mometasone), which inhibits local inflammatory cytokine release and inflammatory cell influx.

cards.q: A patient with birch pollen allergy experiences localized itching and tingling of the lips and soft palate after eating raw apples and peaches. What is the mechanism of this condition?
cards.a: Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Allergy Syndrome), caused by IgE cross-reactivity between airborne pollen proteins (e.g., Bet v 1 in birch) and homologous heat-labile proteins in raw fruits/vegetables.

cards.q: A young adult presents with recurrent, severe Neisseria meningitidis infections. Screening tests show decreased CH50 activity. Which complement components are most likely deficient?
cards.a: Deficient Terminal Complement Components (C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9), impairing the formation of the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC / C5b-9).

cards.q: A newborn with tetralogy of Fallot develops tetany. Labs show serum Ca2+ 6.2 mg/dL and elevated serum phosphate. What is the microdeletion and embryological structure failed in development?
cards.a: 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge Syndrome), due to failure of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop, resulting in thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia.

cards.q: A runner experiences generalized pruritus, hives, and wheezing specifically when jogging within 2 hours after eating a meal containing wheat. What is the diagnosis and acute management strategy?
cards.a: Food-Dependent Exercise-Induced Anaphylaxis (FDEIA). Managed acutely with IM epinephrine, and prevented by refraining from exercise for 4 hours after consuming trigger foods (e.g., gliadin/wheat).

cards.q: A 42-year-old patient with severe asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis presents with peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), skin nodules, and eosinophilia > 15%. Serology is positive for MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA). What vasculitis is this?
cards.a: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss syndrome), a small-to-medium vessel necrotizing vasculitis. Eosinophilic myocarditis is the primary cause of mortality.

cards.q: Compare Pemphigus Vulgaris and Bullous Pemphigoid by target antigen, blister description, and mucosal involvement.
cards.a:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris: Autoantibodies against desmoglein-1 / desmoglein-3 (desmosomes). Blisters are flaccid, easily ruptured, and mucosal involvement is common.
• Bullous Pemphigoid: Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes (dystrophin BP180/BP230). Blisters are tense, pruritic, and mucosal involvement is rare.

cards.q: Compare Pemphigus Vulgaris and Bullous Pemphigoid by Nikolsky Sign and immunofluorescence pattern.
cards.a:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris: Nikolsky positive (gentle rubbing sloughs skin). Immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG/C3 in a 'net-like' / chicken-wire pattern.
• Bullous Pemphigoid: Nikolsky negative. Immunofluorescence shows IgG/C3 deposition in a linear band along the basement membrane zone.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology, body surface area threshold, and clinical management of SJS vs. TEN?
cards.a:
Severe, life-threatening drug reaction causing widespread keratinocyte apoptosis.

Thresholds:
• Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS): < 10% body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment.
• SJS/TEN Overlap: 10–30% BSA.
• Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): > 30% BSA.
Management: Immediate discontinuation of offending drug, admission to a burn unit, supportive fluid resuscitation; Nikolsky positive, mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals).

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor for cutaneous Melanoma, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Prognostic Factor: Breslow Depth (thickness of the tumor in millimeters from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest tumor cell).
• Management: Wide local excision with surgical margins determined by Breslow depth. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is indicated for depth ≥ 0.8 mm.

cards.q: What are the ABCDE criteria for screening suspicious pigmented lesions for melanoma?
cards.a:
• A: Asymmetry.
• B: Border irregularity.
• C: Color variation (multiple shades).
• D: Diameter ≥ 6 mm.
• E: Evolving (changing in size, shape, color, or symptoms like itching/bleeding).

cards.q: What is Psoriasis Vulgaris, and what are the classic clinical signs on exam?
cards.a:
Chronic inflammatory skin disease mediated by Th17/IL-17.

Signs: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees).
• Koebner Phenomenon: New plaques forming at sites of skin trauma.
• Auspitz Sign: Pinpoint bleeding when silvery scales are scraped off.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema) by age group.
cards.a:
Mnemonic: 'Itch that rashes.' Pruritic, erythematous, dry skin.
• Infants: Affects the face, scalp, and extensor surfaces of limbs.
• Children/Adults: Affects the flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae), neck, and hands.

cards.q: What is Erythema Multiforme, and what are its most common etiologies?
cards.a:
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction presenting with classic targetoid lesions (three zones: dusky center, pale ring, erythematous halo) on extremities.

Etiologies: Most commonly triggered by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Mycoplasma pneumoniae; can also be drug-induced (sulfas, anticonvulsants).

cards.q: What clinical conditions are associated with Acanthosis Nigricans?
cards.a:
Hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in intertriginous areas (axilla, neck).

Associations: Insulin resistance (diabetes, obesity, PCOS). If sudden, severe, and eruptive, it indicates Gastric Adenocarcinoma (malignant acanthosis nigricans).

cards.q: What is Rosacea, and how do you differentiate it from Acne Vulgaris?
cards.a:
Inflammatory dermatosis presenting with facial flushing, telangiectasias, papules, and pustules on cheeks/nose. Chronic cases lead to rhinophyma (bulbous nose).

Differentiating Feature: Rosacea is characterized by the absence of comedones (blackheads/whiteheads), which are required for the diagnosis of acne.

cards.q: What is the enzyme defect, clinical presentation, and triggers of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)?
cards.a:
Deficiency of Uroporphyrinogen Decarboxylase (UROD).

Presentation: Painful, blistering, and fragile skin in sun-exposed areas (back of hands), leading to hyperpigmentation, scarring, and facial hypertrichosis (excessive hair). Urine glows coral-red under Wood's lamp.
Triggers: Alcohol, estrogen, iron overload, and strongly associated with Hepatitis C infection.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of Leser-Trélat Sign?
cards.a: Sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses (benign 'stuck-on' waxy lesions). Indicates an underlying internal malignancy (most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma) as a paraneoplastic syndrome.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and histologic description of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)?
cards.a:
Most common skin cancer. Slow-growing, rarely metastasizes.

Presentation: Pearly nodule with telangiectasias (prominent blood vessels) and central ulceration ('rodent ulcer') on sun-exposed head/neck.
Histology: Palisading nuclei at the periphery of tumor nests.

cards.q: What is Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) of the skin, its precursor lesion, and histology?
cards.a:
Second most common skin cancer. Has metastatic potential.

Precursor: Actinic Keratosis (rough, scaly, sand-paper feel plaque on sun-exposed skin).
Presentation: Ulcerated, scaling, or keratotic nodule/plaque. Histology shows keratin pearls.

cards.q: What is Dermatitis Herpetiformis, its autoantibody target, and treatment of choice?
cards.a:
Extremely pruritic vesicular eruption on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). Strongly associated with Celiac Disease.

Pathophysiology: IgA antibodies react against epidermal transglutaminase, depositing as granular IgA in dermal papillae.
Treatment: Gluten-free diet + oral Dapsone (provides rapid symptomatic relief).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and etiologies of Erythema Nodosum.
cards.a:
Inflammatory panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat).

Presentation: Painful, erythematous, tender nodules on the anterior shins.
Etiologies: Idiopathic, Strep infection, Sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome), IBD, Coccidioidomycosis, and drugs (oral contraceptives, sulfonamides).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of Scabies?
cards.a:
Infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei mites.

Presentation: Intense nocturnal generalized pruritus with linear burrows in the web spaces of fingers/wrists, axillae, and groin.
Diagnosis: Skin scraping demonstrating mites, eggs, or scybala (feces) under microscopy.
Treatment: Topical Permethrin 5% cream (applied from neck down, washed off after 8–14 hours, repeated in 1 week) OR oral Ivermectin. Treat all close contacts.

cards.q: What is Pityriasis Rosea, and what is its typical course?
cards.a:
Self-limiting inflammatory dermatosis. Often associated with HHV-6 or HHV-7.

Presentation: Starts with a single, large 2-10 cm 'Herald Patch' on the trunk, followed 1-2 weeks later by a generalized eruption of smaller oval plaques along skin cleavage lines in a 'Christmas Tree' distribution.
Course: Self-limiting; resolves spontaneously in 4–8 weeks; symptomatic treatment.

cards.q: What are the 5 Ps of Lichen Planus, and what key clinical associations exist?
cards.a:
• 5 Ps: Purple, Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar Papules/Plaques, typically on flexor wrists and shins.
• Wickham Striae: Fine white reticular lines on the surface of papules or oral mucosa.
• Association: Strongly associated with Hepatitis C virus.

cards.q: What is Alopecia Areata, its pathophysiology, and diagnostic hair finding?
cards.a:
Autoimmune-mediated hair loss.

Presentation: Smooth, circular, well-demarcated patches of hair loss on the scalp.
Hair Finding: 'Exclamation point' hairs (short, broken hairs that are narrower near the scalp).
Treatment: Intralesional corticosteroids.

cards.q: What is Vitiligo, and how is it clinically evaluated?
cards.a:
Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes causing depigmented patches of skin.

Evaluation: Clinically or using Wood's lamp (depigmented patches show bright blue-white fluorescence). Associated with other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto's, Type 1 DM, Addison's).

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Seborrheic Dermatitis and its first-line treatment.
cards.a:
Inflammatory scaling dermatosis affecting areas with high sebaceous gland density (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, external ear canal). Associated with Malassezia yeast and highly prevalent in Parkinson's disease and HIV.

Presentation: Erythematous plaques with greasy, yellowish scales ('cradle cap' in infants, dandruff in adults).
Treatment: Topical antifungals (ketoconazole shampoo/cream) or low-potency topical steroids.

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of a patient presenting with an expanding, painful, necrotic ulcer with a violaceous, ragged border, often associated with IBD?
cards.a:
Pyoderma Gangrenosum.

Pathophysiology: Neutrophilic dermatosis. Exhibits pathergy (worsens with trauma/biopsy). Associated with IBD, RA, and AML.
Treatment: Systemic Corticosteroids or cyclosporine. Do not perform surgical debridement (pathergy will cause rapid expansion of the ulcer).

cards.q: How is Acne Vulgaris managed in a stepwise manner?
cards.a:
• Mild (comedonal): Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene) + benzoyl peroxide.
• Moderate (inflammatory papules): Add topical antibiotics (clindamycin) or oral antibiotics (doxycycline/sarecycline).
• Severe (nodulocystic / scarring): Oral Isotretinoin (Accutane).

cards.q: What are the critical monitoring and safety rules for initiating oral Isotretinoin (Accutane)?
cards.a:
• Toxicity: Highly teratogenic.
• Safety Rules (iPLEDGE): Requires 2 negative pregnancy tests prior to initiation, monthly pregnancy tests, and use of 2 forms of contraception.
• Monitoring: Baseline and periodic monitoring of fasting lipids and LFTs (causes hypertriglyceridemia and hepatotoxicity).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Tinea Versicolor?
cards.a:
Caused by overgrowth of Malassezia furfur.

Presentation: Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the chest/back that do not tan in summer. KOH prep shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (short hyphae and yeast cells).
Treatment: Topical Selenium Sulfide lotion or topical ketoconazole.

cards.q: What is Erythema Toxicum Neonatorum, and what is the management?
cards.a:
Benign neonatal rash appearing within 24–72 hours of birth. Presents as erythematous macules with central yellow/white pustules on the trunk/extremities, sparing palms and soles. Smear of pustule shows eosinophils.

Management: Reassurance. Self-limiting, resolves in 1–2 weeks.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and treatment of choice for Impetigo?
cards.a:
Superficial bacterial skin infection (usually S. aureus or S. pyogenes).

Presentation: Erythematous macules progressing to vesicles/pustules that rupture, forming honey-colored crusts on the face/mouth.
Treatment: Topical Mupirocin for localized lesions; oral cephalexin for widespread (bullous) impetigo.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of Molluscum Contigiosum, and what pathogen causes it?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Poxvirus.
• Presentation: Firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules with a central dimple. Often self-limiting in children. Widespread facial lesions in adults suggest HIV infection.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with suspected venous stasis dermatitis?
cards.a: Compression therapy, leg elevation, and emollients. Stasis dermatitis is caused by venous hypertension and valve incompetence, presenting as bilateral lower extremity erythema, hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin deposition), and medial malleolus ulcers.

cards.q: Contrast the ulcers of Arterial Insufficiency vs. Venous Insufficiency vs. Neuropathic (Diabetic) disease.
cards.a:
• Arterial: Located on tips of toes / lateral malleolus. Punched-out appearance, pale/necrotic base, very painful, cold skin, absent pulses.
• Venous: Located on medial malleolus. Irregular borders, wet/exudative, hyperpigmentation of surrounding skin, minimally painful, warm skin.
• Neuropathic (Diabetic): Located on pressure points (soles of feet/plantar metatarsal heads). Deep, painless, surrounded by thick callus, warm skin.

cards.q: What is Hidradenitis Suppurativa, and what is its chronic management?
cards.a:
Chronic inflammatory occlusion of follicular infundibulum in apocrine gland-bearing areas (axillae, groin, perineum).

Presentation: Recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, draining sinus tracts, and double-comedones leading to severe scarring.
Management: Topical clindamycin for mild; oral tetracyclines for moderate; TNF inhibitors (adalimumab) or surgical excision of the entire gland-bearing area for severe.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features of Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease) and the causative pathogen.
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Parvovirus B19.
• Presentation: Low-grade fever followed by a bright-red 'slapped-cheek' rash on the face, which then spreads to the body as a reticular, lacy maculopapular eruption.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of roseola infantum (sixth disease), and what pathogen causes it?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: HHV-6 or HHV-7.
• Presentation: High fever (often > 104°F) for 3–5 days in an infant, which resolves abruptly, followed immediately by the onset of a rose-pink maculopapular rash on the trunk spreading to extremities.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with suspected toxic epidermal necrolysis?
cards.a: Discontinue all non-essential medications immediately and admit the patient to an intensive care or burn unit for supportive fluid and electrolyte management.

cards.q: Explain the difference in etiology between a cherry angioma and a strawberry (infantile) hemangioma.
cards.a:
• Cherry Angioma: Benign vascular proliferation in adults. Bright red, small papules, increase with age. Do not regress.
• Strawberry Hemangioma: Benign capillary hemangioma of infancy. Appears within weeks of birth, grows rapidly, and then regresses spontaneously by age 5–9. Treated with beta-blockers (propranolol) if obstructing vision/airway.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for a patient with tinea capitis?
cards.a: Oral Griseofulvin or oral Terbinafine. Topical antifungals are ineffective because they do not penetrate the hair shaft.

cards.q: Describe the diagnostic test and treatment of choice for Intertrigo.
cards.a:
Inflammation of skin folds caused by Candida albicans.

Presentation: Erythematous macerated plaques in groin/axillae/under breasts with satellite lesions (small pustules nearby).
Diagnosis: KOH prep showing pseudohyphae and budding yeast.
Treatment: Topical Nystatin or topical Clotrimazole.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of Actinic Keratosis, and why is it treated?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Small, rough, scaly, erythematous papule with a sandpaper-like feel on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, forearms).
• Why: It is a premalignant lesion that can progress to Squamous Cell Carcinoma. Treated with cryotherapy or topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU).

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of an elderly patient presenting with multiple waxy, stuck-on, brown plaques on the trunk?
cards.a: Seborrheic Keratosis (benign, non-malignant, no treatment required unless irritated).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for a patient presenting with localized Shingles (Herpes Zoster) within 72 hours of symptom onset?
cards.a: Oral Valacyclovir or Famciclovir for 7 days (reduces duration of rash and severity of postherpetic neuralgia).

cards.q: What is the definition of postherpetic neuralgia, and what is the treatment of choice?
cards.a:
• Definition: Persistent pain lasting ≥ 4 months after the resolution of a shingles rash.
• Treatment: Gabapentin, Pregabalin, or Tricyclic Antidepressants (Amitriptyline).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of a keloid?
cards.a:
Hypertrophic scar that extends beyond the borders of the original wound, caused by overproduction of collagen (Type I and III). Common in patients with dark skin.

Management: Intralesional corticosteroid injections (triamcinolone). Surgical excision alone is contraindicated due to high recurrence rates.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of bullous impetigo, and what toxin causes it?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Large, flaccid, fluid-filled bullae that rupture, leaving scaly rim. Occurs in infants/young children.
• Pathogenesis: Caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing exfoliative toxin A, which targets desmoglein-1 (causing intraepidermal cleavage, similar to pemphigus).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and causative pathogen of Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Coxsackievirus A16.
• Presentation: Painful oral ulcers (herpangina) + vesicular lesions on the palms of hands, soles of feet, and buttocks, accompanied by fever.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and management of Pityriasis Versicolor.
cards.a: Malassezia furfur overgrowth. Presents as hypo- or hyperpigmented macules on the upper chest/back that do not tan. Diagnosed by KOH prep showing short septate hyphae and spores. Treated with topical selenium sulfide.

cards.q: What is the definition of Erythroderma (Exfoliative Dermatitis)?
cards.a: Inflammatory skin condition involving ≥ 90% of the body surface area with diffuse erythema and scaling. Can be caused by psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, drug reactions, or cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sezary syndrome). Requires hospitalization for fluid/electrolyte management.

cards.q: Explain the difference in presentation between drug-induced urticaria and serum sickness-like reaction.
cards.a:
• Urticaria: Type I IgE-mediated. Occurs within minutes/hours of drug administration. Presents as transient pruritic wheals.
• Serum Sickness-like Reaction: Type III immune-complex-mediated. Occurs 1-3 weeks after drug administration. Presents with fever, hives/rash, and joint pain.

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of an infant presenting with scaling, yellow, greasy plaques on the scalp?
cards.a: Seborrheic Dermatitis (specifically 'cradle cap').

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for mild localized plaque psoriasis?
cards.a: Topical Corticosteroids (high-potency) + topical Vitamin D analogs (Calcipotriene).
